'''Mark Arthur Reed''' (January 4, 1955 – May 5, 2021) was an American physicist and professor at [[Yale University]]. He is noted particularly for seminal research on [[quantum dots]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Mark A. Reed (1955–2021) |journal=Nature |date=March 24, 2022 |first1=Laurie E. |last1=Calvet |first2=Jia |last2=Chen |first3=Takhee |last3=Lee |first4=Alan |last4=Seabaugh |volume=17 |issue=4 |page=336 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-022-01093-5.pdf |doi=10.1038/s41565-022-01093-5 |pmid=35332295 |s2cid=247633468 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.eng.yale.edu/reedlab/MarkReed.htm |title=Reed Lab @ Yale University: Members |access-date=2008-01-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120207163631/http://www.eng.yale.edu/reedlab/MarkReed.htm|archive-date=2012-02-07 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=On the Shoulders of Giants: 10 Quantum Pioneers of the Past |last1=Lenahan |first1=Brian T. |last2=Hughes-Castleberry |first2=Kenna |chapter=Mark A. Reed: The Quantum Cowboy |pages=164–179 |publisher=Aquitaine Innovation Advisors |date=2023 |isbn=978-1-989478-20-2}}</ref> 
==Career and education==
He coined the term [[quantum dots]],<ref>{{cite journal | journal = [[Physical Review Letters]] | volume = 60 | issue = 6 | pages = 535–537 | doi =  10.1103/PhysRevLett.60.535 |bibcode = 1988PhRvL..60..535R | pmid=10038575 | title=Observation of discrete electronic states in a zero-dimensional semiconductor nanostructure | date=February 1988| last1 = Reed | first1 = M. | last2 = Randall | first2 = J. | last3 = Aggarwal | first3 = R. | last4 = Matyi | first4 = R. | last5 = Moore | first5 = T. | last6 = Wetsel | first6 = A. }}</ref> for demonstrating the first zero-dimensional electronic device that had fully quantized energy states.  Reed did research in electronic transport in nanoscale and [[Mesoscopic physics|mesoscopic systems]], artificially structured materials and devices, molecular electronics, biosensors and bioelectronic systems, and nanofluidics. He was the author of more than 200 publications, had given over 75 plenary and over 400 invited talks, and held 33 U.S. and foreign patents on quantum effect, heterojunction, and molecular devices.  He was the editor in chief of the journal ''[[Nanotechnology (journal)|Nanotechnology]]'' (2009–2019) and of the journal ''Nano Futures'', and held numerous other editorial and advisory board positions. 
Reed received his Ph.D. from [[Syracuse University]] in 1983. He worked at [[Texas Instruments]] from 1983 to 1990, where he demonstrated the first quantum dot device.  He had been at [[Yale School of Engineering & Applied Science|Yale School of Engineering and Applied Science]] since 1990, where he held the Harold Hodgkinson Chair of Engineering and Applied Science. Notable work there included the first conductance measurement of a single molecule,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reed |first=M. A.|date=October 10, 1997 |title=Conductance of a Molecular Junction|journal=Science|volume=278|issue=5336|pages=252–254|doi=10.1126/science.278.5336.252|s2cid=97922206}}</ref> the first single molecule transistor,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Song|first1=Hyunwook|last2=Kim|first2=Youngsang|last3=Jang|first3=Yun Hee|last4=Jeong|first4=Heejun|last5=Reed|first5=Mark A.|last6=Lee|first6=Takhee|date=December 2009|title=Observation of molecular orbital gating|journal=Nature|volume=462|issue=7276|pages=1039–1043|doi=10.1038/nature08639|pmid=20033044|s2cid=4308859|issn=0028-0836}}</ref> and the development of CMOS nanowire biosensors.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stern|first1=Eric|last2=Klemic|first2=James F.|last3=Routenberg|first3=David A.|last4=Wyrembak|first4=Pauline N.|last5=Turner-Evans|first5=Daniel B.|last6=Hamilton|first6=Andrew D.|last7=LaVan|first7=David A.|last8=Fahmy|first8=Tarek M.|last9=Reed|first9=Mark A.|date=February 2007|title=Label-free immunodetection with CMOS-compatible semiconducting nanowires|journal=Nature|volume=445|issue=7127|pages=519–522|doi=10.1038/nature05498|pmid=17268465|s2cid=205211233|issn=0028-0836}}</ref>
==Awards and recognition==
Reed had been elected to the Connecticut Academy of Science and Engineering and Who's Who in the World.  His awards included; Fortune Magazine “Most Promising Young Scientist” (1990), the Kilby Young Innovator Award (1994), the Fujitsu ISCS Quantum Device Award (2001), the Yale Science and Engineering Association Award for Advancement of Basic and Applied Science (2002), Fellow of the American Physical Society (2002), the inaugural IEEE Pioneer Award in Nanotechnology (2007),<ref>{{cite web |title=2007 Awardees |publisher=IEEE Nanotechnology Council |access-date=September 10, 2023 |url=https://ieeenano.org/awards/2007-awardees}}</ref> Fellow of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (2009), and a Finalist for the World Technology Award (2010).

==Personal life==
He married Elizabeth Schaefer on August 24, 1996. He died on May 5, 2021.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hahamy |first1=Madison |title=Mark Reed, Director of Undergraduate Studies for Electrical Engineering, dies at 66 |url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2021/05/07/mark-reed-director-of-undergraduate-studies-for-electrical-engineering-dies-at-66/ |access-date=7 May 2021 |work=Yale Daily News}}</ref>
